title: The best maths worksheet ever?
author: Craig Barton
summary: Barton champions a reusable worksheet structure built on the question taxonomy of Pointon and Sangwin (2003), illustrated with a highest-common-factor example from Dan Lewis. The eight question types run from factual recall and routine calculation through classifying, interpreting, proving, extending, constructing examples and criticising a fallacy. His argument is that most worksheets stop at routine calculation, whereas this structure checks depth of understanding and builds reasoning and mathematical communication. He adds further examples from Middleton Maths, suggests uses as low-stakes assessment, homework or paired work, and invites readers to build one for an upcoming topic.
points: A worksheet that moves through eight deliberately different question types tests understanding far more broadly than a page of routine calculations.
Classifying examples against non-examples and constructing your own example under constraints are presented as better routes into a concept than technical definitions.
Giving the answer and asking what can be inferred about the question reverses the usual direction of work and prompts interpretation.
Criticising a fallacy requires students to communicate mathematically, and adding an instruction to explain how they would help the fictional student goes further.
The structure is time-consuming to produce, so Barton suggests departments each build one worksheet and share them.
quotes: Factual recall needs to come before carrying out a procedure. Do students know what they are actually trying to work out? Do they have the prerequisite knowledge to engage with the new idea?
This is the most common question type on most worksheets. And for good reason, because fluency in carrying out calculations is important. But there is a lot more to maths than this.
I am not a huge fan of technical definitions. I much prefer the challenge to classify. Can students sort the examples from the non-examples given some criteria?

The idea of giving the answer and asking what you can infer about the question is a powerful one, flipping the usual way of working on its head. Similarly, we could challenge students to interpret a situation by adding a context to the question that students need to unpick to get at the mathematics.
Proof does not need to be in the formal, algebraic sense. But questions like these encourage students to try examples in a logical, systematic way as they construct their arguments.

Identifying and explaining mistakes is so important. Not only do they challenge students to think beyond carrying out a routine, but in their quest to interpret someone else’s work, they must also communicate mathematically.

This structure could be used as a low-stakes assessment, a homework, or an independent task followed by paired collaboration. It is a great way of checking the depth of students’ understanding, and promoting key skills such as reasoning, conjecturing and mathematical communication.
